q-0394.answer: Scholars classify the 114 surahs by where they were first revealed: approximately **86 surahs are Meccan** (revealed before Hijrah in Makkah) and **28 are Medinan** (revealed after Hijrah in Madinah). Meccan surahs often focus on faith, tawhid, and the Hereafter; Medinan surahs often address law, community, and governance. Individual surah pages show each surah's revelation type.

q-0552.answer:
Surah At-Taghaabun (64) — Mutual Disillusion · 18 ayahs · Medinan

Main teachings:
• He is the One Who has control over all creation, the One praised for all He created and decreed.
• Whatever you spend, then Allah will replace it, and on Him will be the reward of whatever you give away in charity.
• Allah created you with these characteristics and He willed that for you.
• Give from what Allah has granted you to your relatives, the poor, the needy and the weak.

Full ayah text and tafsir are available in the sources below.

Surah Al-Balad (90) — The City · 20 ayahs · Meccan

Main teachings:
• Man is encompassed by Allah and His Bounties
• He was from the believers who worked righteous deeds, and advised each other to be patient with the harms of the people, and to be merciful with them.
• Then, along with these beautiful and pure characteristics, he was a believer in his heart, seeking the reward of that from Allah.
• It will be sealed over them and there will be no way for them to avoid it, nor will they have any way out.

c-0068.answer:
The major contemporary fiqh councils permit it — as an act the Quran's own idiom exalts: "Whoever saves a life, it is as if he saved all mankind" (5:32). The Islamic Fiqh Academy (OIC, Resolution 26, 1988) approved both living donation (where it doesn't gravely harm the donor — donating a kidney, part of a liver, blood) and cadaveric donation (with prior consent of the deceased or the family's), prohibiting only the SALE of organs — the body is a trust to give from, never a commodity. Similar rulings came from al-Azhar, the Saudi Council of Senior Scholars (Resolution 99, 1982), and for Western Muslims, detailed treatments like the UK's 2019 fatwa by Mufti Zubair Butt, which also works through brain-death criteria.

The instinctive objection — that the body is sacred and must return whole — is answered within the tradition itself: sanctity is precisely why donation is noble, giving from what is honored; jurists invoke the principle that necessity permits and that saving life outranks preserving tissue after death, just as eating carrion is permitted to the starving (2:173). A minority of scholars, particularly in the Indian subcontinent tradition, remain opposed — a position to respect. But the mainstream global verdict stands: donating is permitted and rewarded, receiving is permitted, and registering as a donor can be your final sadaqah — a stranger breathing, seeing or living through what you left behind.
sources: Saudi Senior Scholars Resolution 99 (1982); Mufti Zubair Butt, UK organ donation fatwa (2019)
